leads.name: Yayoi Sugi
leads.why: FALLEN. Toppled by a typhoon in August 2023. yakushima-tour.com states it plainly: 'The Yayoi cedar tree was toppled by a typhoon in August 2023', adding that it can still be seen up close where it lies. Roughly 2,000 years old, about 20 minutes on foot from the Shiratani Unsuikyo trailhead, and it was one of the island's best known named cedars. It is a fallen trunk, so it is never an entry here, however famous. It may appear inside another tree's story as context. Recorded so no future pass rediscovers it: a general search still returns it described in the present tense as a living attraction, which is exactly how a dead tree gets published.

leads.name: Wilson's Stump (Wilson Kabu)
leads.why: A STUMP. The tree was felled around 1586 and what remains is a vast hollow stump you can stand inside, with a heart-shaped opening to the sky. One of Yakushima's most famous sights and never an entry here, because this site sends people to living trees. Good context inside another story. RE-CONFIRMED 2026-09-04 (famousjapan-batch-e1 pass, candidate from Commons category _famous-japan, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wilson_Stump_01.jpg and related files): felled to supply timber for Kyoto's Hoko-ji great-Buddha hall; trunk circumference 13.8m, hollow interior about 16 sq m with a small shrine inside; named after botanist Ernest Henry Wilson, who documented it in 1914. No evidence of a living tree growing from within the stump itself; sources describe three descendant cedars growing nearby as separate, independently rooted trees rather than regrowth from this stump's own root system, so this stays blocked rather than being treated as a live-regrowth case like Ikiki no Gomon on Omishima (data/research/famousjapan-batch-e1-verified.json).
